item.title: Conversation about Plausible Fiction at ACT2026
item.description: A recollection of conversation with David Spivak, the creator of Plausible Fiction at ACT2026.
item.content:encoded:
1 Conversation about Plausible Fiction at ACT2026

Keywords: applied category theory, musing, polynomial functors, blog

Summary: A recollection of conversation with David Spivak, the creator of Plausible Fiction at ACT2026.

At ACT 2026, I spoke with David Spivak about his idea of Plausible Fiction. While it is still a very early concept, David’s IPAM Talk gave a very nice overview of the work. Based on my recollection and notes from our conversation, the way he suggested to think about a plausible fiction is like a flow chart or as the “mathematics of a self-fulfilling prophecy”. An example he gave was, “suppose there is a task you want to do such as, ’we will make a national highway for the United States.”’ Accordingly, the outcomes for each step taken to achieve this goal are effectively a height one tree on a polynomial (i.e. a corolla) which could be explored further in the textbook, Polynomial Functors: A Mathematical Theory of Interaction.

As I recall from my conversation with David, this process can be interpreted as the kleisli category of the free monad on Poly to your desired goal or outcome. Each of these corollas can be thought of as directed rooted graphs ascending upwards, where each branch coming from a node of this tree represents a decision path. You can then recursively add these corollas “upwards” as you continue progressing up the tree and branching out from each end of a branch on your graph. The whole tree itself may have arbitrary heights like a binary tree does and does not have to be balanced and certainly does not have to have a height of one. An important aspect of this branching is that these trees of decisions do not require any particular resolution. You can define subtasks as granularly or coarsely as required to denote and achieve a goal.

When considering examples of plausible fictions, the example of “make a national highway,” actually comes from US President Eisenhower. David mentioned how the concept of a plausible fiction most directly applies to and is most readily understood by a goal or desired outcome described by an authority or individual figure leading an effort. Such an entity would then define and direct the progress related to a specific goal.

It may be a surprise to note that President Eisenhower, was, in fact, no civil engineer. Instead, what Eisenhower did and what plausible fiction allows, is the ability to make a critiquable, shared vision. When Eisenhower declared his goal for a national highway, there was no exact path to achieve this goal. Yet, he had plenty of advisors and aides who could help contribute their expertise to fill in all the necessary pieces along the way to that goal. Similarly, plausible fiction allows individuals with different skillsets to help the creator of the plausible fiction describe and address the gaps of a fiction with more details. In a way, plausible fiction can be thought of as an invitation to actualization.

Moving from historical to personal examples, David pointed out that a personal anecdote I shared would qualify as a plausible fiction. This anecdote was, and is, my nebulous goal of “bringing and applying category theory to public health.” In particular, the reasonable detailed progression of:

1.
Gradually moving from biomedical engineering and health informatics into applied mathematics
2.
Receiving support and supervision to investigate applied category theory
3.
Advance sufficiently to present at both ACT 2025 and ACT 2026 constitute components of a plausible fiction.

And while these pieces are no longer fiction but reality, there is still much work to be done to achieve my long-term plausible fiction!

To conclude our discussion, another example we discussed was considering health systems. Thinking about sweeping, general improvements to a health system would be an underspecified plausible fiction and hard to take action on. The reason being is that it is hard to imagine what an “improved” health system would be as right now, the goal is too broad. However, building on this, a future discussion could consider from a health informaticist’s point of view of what could be a valid plausible fiction in a health system. Perhaps imagining something like, “I will define how to make health informatics research studies composable,” might be a fun place to start!

I would like to express thanks to David Spivak for the discussion and some clarifications about the concept of Plausible Fiction!

How To Cite

Zelko, Jacob S. Conversation about Plausible Fiction at ACT2026. https://jacobzelko.com/notes/aaa-0295/. October 26, 2026.

item.title: Data Fabrics ACT 2025 Proposal
item.description: Original proposal about data fabrics for ACT 2025.
item.content:encoded:
1 Data Fabrics ACT 2025 Proposal

Keywords: applied category theory, data fabric

Summary: Original proposal about data fabrics for ACT 2025.

Matt Cuffaro, Sean L. Wu, and I wrote this proposal for ACT 2025 which gives a concise overview and motivation for data fabrics:

Robust data science frameworks are those which can adapt to complex, evolving threats in public health. While the OMOP Common Data Model (OMOP CDM) provides an international standard for recording patient electronic health records, such datasets, like patient health records, census survey microdata, health system indicators, and environmental data, requires coordination to federate this data so that it is consumed in a timely way. However, delays from integrating and analyzing these datasets can have severe implications within a public health crisis.

To address these challenges in data integration and analysis, novel mathematical approaches that can handle complex relationships while maintaining computational efficiency are increasingly necessary. We turn our attention to AlgebraicJulia, an open-source ecosystem of Julia packages operating under the philosophy that applied category theory provides a mathematical basis for reasoning about the design and construction of scientific software. The central data structure, the “attributed C-Set,” (ACSet), defined in [2], has diverse and ubiquitous application throughout AlgebraicJulia, from specifying multiphysics models to defining large meshes. However as an in-memory columnar database, it is restricted by the RAM specifications of the client machine, and, by an analogy between database tables and objects in a category, makes large schema (such as the OMOP CDM) difficult to specify. Large (up to terabyte-sized) datasets and complex schema makes working with existing workflows more attractive and in turn slows adoption of AlgebraicJulia tools by working scientists in more data-intensive fields, such as public health.

Our response to the general problem of ergonomically specifying large database schema, as well as the specific challenge of handling the schema and data of the OMOP CDM in the AlgebraicJulia framework takes inspiration from the data fabric, or federated database architectures which provide a unified access protocol for accessing, mutating, and collating data [1]. They were originally developed in order to manage growing data models that were increasingly becoming distributed and mediated by microservices, but have recently found application in academic science [3], [4] We will demonstrate how our implementation of a data fabric meets our requirements of (1) quickly specifying a large database schema which (2) may be decomposed into smaller schema populated by different data sources which (3) may be queried and manipulated through a common access protocol. We borrow an industry term, ”data fabric,” to call our contribution, which is a diagram of ACSets, whose nodes are data sources and edges are foreign key constraints between data sources, which also has database reflection and virtualization, or caching of data.

In this talk we will give an exposition of ACSets and the use-case from public health, specifying the OMOP CDM, to motivate our implementation of the “data fabric.” As a use case example, we will demonstrate how such a framework could assist in the analysis of climate-impacted diseases such as heart attack by integrating this patient data with environmental and census data. Our intent is to show that with relatively little developer time, we can replicate important features from enterprise and scientific uses in databases into an open-source ecosystem while remaining both consistent with the design philosophy of AlgebraicJulia and interoperable with the broader Julia scientific ecosystem. A category-theoretic perspective, by mathematically formalizing what it means to think about database specification and transformation, gives an additional layer of abstraction that helps us reason about the practical challenges in federating data. We argue that this abstraction helps us develop a robust framework for data management in open-source, mathematically-guided science.

References

[1]

T. Priebe, S. Neumaier, and S. Markus, “Finding your way through the jungle of big data architectures,” in 2021 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (Big Data), IEEE, 2021, pp. 5994–5996.

[2]

E. Patterson, O. Lynch, and J. Fairbanks, “Categorical data structures for technical computing,” Compositionality, vol. 4, 2022.

[3]

I. Buleje, V. S. Siu, K. Y. Hsieh, et al., “A versatile data fabric for advanced IoT-based remote health monitoring,” in 2023 IEEE International Conference on Digital Health (ICDH), IEEE, 2023, pp. 88–90.

[4]

A. Panta, X. Huang, N. McCurdy, et al., “Web-based visualization and analytics of petascale data: Equity as a tide that lifts all boats,” in 2024 Ieee 14th Symposium on Large Data Analysis and Visualization (Ldav), IEEE, 2024, pp. 1–11.

How To Cite

item.description: Some overviews of causality from different fields
item.content:encoded:
1 Types of Causality

Keywords: causality, order theory

Summary: Some overviews of causality from different fields

This is just a quick stubbed out note and loose grouping to try and define what is referred to as “causality”.

Basically, there are many different flavors of causality and it is not clear what is meant by them. It confuses me to no end the types of causality that exist – not from a strictly philosophical or quantitative dimension but even in colloquial speech. In my mind, the most accessible and common way of talking about causality is using order theory:

Which could be said in multiple different ways as “A before B”, “B after A”, or “A precedes B”. All it requires is that there is an order between two things. What this order operator, ≤, is exactly and what A and B are do not really matter so much to me.

My friend Oscar Smith and I have spoken about this in the context of differential equations and dynamical systems modelling but I haven’t had much a chance to dig deeper into it. Moreover, Nate Osgood and I have also reflected on the fact that causality can also mean something extremely different in the social and health sciences. And even still in quantum mathematics, there is a whole slew of literature about causality. To me, it seems like every field has a particular subtlety with their definition.
